questions.stem: James Davidson, 75, sees you in general practice with 4 to 5 months of progressive dry cough, exertional breathlessness and weight loss. He has never smoked. You ask about his work and he says only, "I was a builder, from the late 1960s through the 1970s." What is the most important follow-up question to ask next?
options: "Have you ever kept pet birds or pigeons at home?"
"Have you travelled overseas or been in contact with anyone with TB?"
"Were you ever exposed to asbestos, dust or fibres in your work?"
"Has your ramipril dose been changed in the last few months?"
questions.why: A builder from the 1960s and 1970s needs a direct question about asbestos, dust and fibres. "I was a builder" is not enough. Asbestos causes lung cancer, mesothelioma and asbestosis decades later, even in people who have never smoked, and the exposure should be documented in case of a later compensation claim.
notes: Bird exposure points to hypersensitivity pneumonitis. It is worth asking about, but the job history he has just given makes asbestos the key exposure to clarify.
TB risk matters with an apical lesion, but it does not follow on from his occupation, and his weight loss and hoarseness point first to occupational malignancy.
ACE inhibitor cough is a diagnosis of exclusion. It cannot explain his weight loss or breathlessness, and asking about it does not follow up his work history.

questions.stem: Mr Davidson, 75, a never smoker with past asbestos exposure, has a 6 cm right apical mass on chest X-ray. He is stable, with SpO2 95% at rest and eGFR 70. Along with phoning a respiratory physician today, which investigation should you arrange next from general practice?
options: Repeat chest X-ray in 6 weeks after a course of amoxicillin
Urgent contrast CT of the chest and upper abdomen
High-resolution non-contrast CT of the chest for interstitial disease
Sputum cytology on three early-morning samples
questions.why: A chest X-ray suspicious for lung cancer needs an urgent contrast CT of the chest and upper abdomen to stage the tumour (nodes, liver, adrenals). Under the Optimal Care Pathway he should also be referred to be seen within 2 weeks, without waiting for the CT result. His eGFR of 70 allows contrast.
notes: He has no fever and no sputum, and the cough has built up over months. A trial of antibiotics with a repeat film only delays the work-up of a likely malignancy.
HRCT looks for interstitial disease such as asbestosis. It does not stage a mass, and without contrast it shows the mediastinum and hila poorly.
His cough is dry, and sputum cytology is insensitive, especially for peripheral lesions. It is no substitute for CT and a biopsy.

questions.stem: Mr Davidson, 75, has a likely lung malignancy. His bloods show Hb 121 g/L with a normal MCV, platelets 412 x 10^9/L, WCC normal, CRP 14 mg/L and albumin 33 g/L. Which mechanism best explains his anaemia?
options: Vitamin B12 deficiency from his reduced dietary intake
Occult gastrointestinal blood loss causing iron deficiency
Tumour infiltration of the marrow replacing red cell production
Hepcidin rise driven by IL-6, trapping iron in macrophages
questions.why: In anaemia of chronic disease, inflammatory cytokines (mainly IL-6) make the liver release more hepcidin. Hepcidin breaks down ferroportin, so iron stays locked in macrophages and enterocytes. The result is a normocytic anaemia with low serum iron, normal or high ferritin, and often a reactive thrombocytosis.
notes: B12 deficiency gives a macrocytic anaemia, but his MCV is normal. Body stores of B12 also last years, so a few months of poor appetite would not deplete them.
He has no GI symptoms, and chronic blood loss would tend to cause a microcytic picture. A rising CRP and low albumin point to inflammation instead.
Marrow infiltration usually causes several cytopenias or a leukoerythroblastic film. His platelets are raised and his white count is normal.

questions.stem: Mr Davidson, 75, has a 6 cm right apical lung mass that abuts the apical pleura, and his voice has become hoarse over the past 1 to 2 months. Given its course near the right lung apex, which nerve is most likely involved?
options: Right recurrent laryngeal nerve, looping under the right subclavian artery
Left recurrent laryngeal nerve, looping under the arch of the aorta, behind the trachea
Right phrenic nerve, descending on the front of anterior scalene
Right external laryngeal nerve, running with the superior thyroid artery
questions.why: The right recurrent laryngeal nerve leaves the vagus and hooks under the right subclavian artery, right next to the cervical pleura at the lung apex. A right apical (Pancoast) tumour can involve it and paralyse the right vocal cord, causing hoarseness.
notes: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch in the mediastinum. Left hilar or aortopulmonary window lesions involve it, not a right apical mass.
The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm. Involvement causes a raised hemidiaphragm and breathlessness, not hoarseness.
The external laryngeal nerve runs in the neck, well above the lung apex. It supplies cricothyroid, so damage mainly affects pitch rather than causing hoarseness.
